title: Tax havens explained
subtitle: $10 trillion in hiding
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: About 10% of the world's wealth escapes tax in secretive territories. How does the system work, and why does it survive so well?

hero.hook: The Cayman Islands have 65,000 residents and more than 100,000 companies. Welcome to the world of tax havens.

blocks.text: Some territories, often tiny ones, let companies and great fortunes escape almost all the tax they owe at home. These are **tax havens**. An estimated $10 trillion, roughly 8 to 10% of the world's wealth, sits in them.

This is not only a problem for accountants. It deprives states of $600 billion a year, money that could have paid for hospitals or schools. Here is how this discreet system works, and why it resists regulation so well.

A tax haven rests on three pillars: taxes close to zero, deep secrecy, and very little cooperation with other countries. Territories like these attract capital from all over the world, in what is known as the [[offshore]] economy.

In several of them you can set up a shell company: a business with no office and no employees, existing only on paper. Its one purpose is usually to hide the identity of the person who really owns the money, the beneficial owner.

blocks.caption: The Cayman Islands, one of the largest financial centers in the world despite their small size

blocks.text: The Cayman Islands have only 65,000 residents, but more than 100,000 companies are registered there. That makes them the world's fifth-largest financial center for bank deposits, on a territory smaller than Paris.

sections.title: The art of making a profit disappear

blocks.text: For large companies the goal is not necessarily illegal. It is called **tax optimization**: using each country's rules cleverly in order to pay less. The main tool is [[transfer pricing]], where a company sets the price of the trades between its own subsidiaries, so that its profits show up where the tax is lowest.

A common method is to move a brand or a patent to a subsidiary based in a tax haven. The other subsidiaries, in France for example, then have to pay huge sums for the right to use that brand. Those payments cut their taxable profit locally, while inflating it in the tax haven.
The French phrase for a tax haven, “paradis fiscal,” comes from a mistranslation. English says “haven,” a safe harbor for money, not “heaven.” Two words that sound alike changed the meaning.

The financial crisis of 2008, then the publication of the [[Panama Papers]] in 2016, set off a wave of outrage. Under pressure from the OECD and the G20, banks must now pass information about their foreign clients to tax authorities automatically.

The biggest step forward came in 2021, with an international deal setting a minimum tax rate of 15% for multinationals. The idea is to stop countries from competing by cutting their taxes without end to attract companies. If a firm pays only 5% in a tax haven, its home country can now claim the remaining 10%.
When the largest fortunes escape tax, the middle class and small local businesses carry a bigger share of the burden. Public services such as health and education are weakened too, for lack of money.

The battle is now moving to the digital world. Online platforms no longer need offices to make money in a country, which makes tax borders more and more porous. Tax authorities now use big data to spot anomalies, and campaigners want public registers showing who really owns each company.

Tax havens hold about 10% of the world's wealth, thanks to banking secrecy and taxes close to zero. Since 2021 a global minimum tax rate of 15% has tried to limit this flight of capital, but the battle is far from won.
